
JSR only. On npm, the same command is the `polytini` bin.

`types/cli.d.ts`:

```ts
// The polytini command. Running it is the whole API.

export {};
```

## API

### Usage

```js
import { encode, decode, decodeFlat, encodeFlat, decodeLatLng, toGeoJSON, fromGeoJSON } from '@duoquote/polytini';

decode(str, 6);                              // precision 6, for OSRM polyline6 or Valhalla
decode(str, { precision: 6, order: 'lnglat' }); // [lng, lat] tuples
encode(points, { factor: 1e5 });             // a factor instead of a precision
encode([{ lat: 38.5, lng: -120.2 }]);        // objects work too: lat/latitude, lng/lon/longitude
decodeLatLng(str);                           // [{ lat, lng }], for Google Maps and Leaflet
toGeoJSON(str);                              // { type: 'LineString', coordinates: [[lng, lat], ...] }
fromGeoJSON(lineStringOrFeature);
decodeFlat(str);                             // one Float64Array [lat0, lng0, lat1, lng1, ...]
encodeFlat(new Float64Array([38.5, -120.2]));
```

Options are a number (the precision) or an object:

- `precision`: decimal places, 0 to 15. Default 5.
- `factor`: multiply by this instead of `10 ** precision`.
- `order`: `'latlng'` (default) or `'lnglat'`. The string itself always stores latitude first; this only changes the tuples you pass in and get back.
- `strict`: default `true`. See below.
- `onIssue`: with `strict: false`, a function that gets each error strict mode would have thrown. See [below](#reporting-what-lenient-mode-skipped).
- `dimensions`: values per point, 1 to 16. Default 2. GraphHopper puts elevation third.
- `zFactor`: the factor for the third and later values, like GraphHopper's elevation multiplier of 100.

The precision isn't stored in the string, so both sides have to agree. A precision 6 string decoded at precision 5 gives coordinates ten times too big, with no error.

#### Strict mode

By default, malformed input throws a `PolylineError` with a `code` and, where it makes sense, an `index`:

- `char`: a character outside `?` to `~` (index of the character)
- `truncated`: the string ends inside a value or a point
- `overflow`: a value past 2^53, where Number math stops being exact
- `coordinate`: NaN, Infinity, `null` or a missing coordinate in encode (index of the point)
- `input`: not a string or an array
- `option`: a bad option

```js
decode('_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnq');                    // throws PolylineError: Truncated at 17 (code 'truncated')
decode('_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnq', { strict: false }); // [[38.5, -120.2]]
```

With `strict: false` it never throws on bad data: decode skips invalid characters and drops an incomplete last point, and encode treats missing or non-finite coordinates as 0.

#### Reporting what lenient mode skipped

`onIssue` tells you what `strict: false` skipped over, so you can decode a broken string and still say what was wrong with it, without decoding it twice:

```js
const issues = [];
decode('_p~iF~ps|U_ul LnnqC_mqNvxq`', { strict: false, onIssue: (e) => issues.push(e) });
// [[38.5, -120.2], [40.7, -120.95]]
// issues: PolylineError 'char' at 13, then 'truncated' at 27
```

It gets a `PolylineError`, created and not thrown, for each problem: every invalid character, every value past 2^53 (once, at the character where it passes), and a string that ends inside a value or a point (once, at the end). The first one is exactly the error strict mode throws for that input: the same code, index and message. Later ones have their index in the input as it is, not in what's left after skipping. Usually there's just one.

Decoding goes on after `onIssue` returns, and the output is the same as `strict: false` without it. To stop at the first problem, throw from it; decode then throws your error. With `strict: true` it's never called, and encode doesn't call it.

Every decoder that takes `strict` takes it: `decode`, `decodeFlat`, `decodeLatLng`, `toGeoJSON` and the presets on every entry, `/wasm` (`decodeMany` reports each line's issues with the index in that line), the integrations that decode, `/stream` (the index is in the whole input, wherever the chunks were cut, and the line decoders add the 1-based `line`) and `/flexible`, which now takes `{ strict: false, onIssue }` too. Its header is always strict, because nothing after it can be read without it. `/lite` has no lenient mode, so it has no `onIssue` either.

It costs nothing when you don't use it: only the slow decoder that already handles bad input reads it, so decoding valid input runs the same code as before. In paired runs against 0.1.7 on Node 24, Bun, Deno and Chrome the difference stayed inside the noise of 0.1.7 against itself ([CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)). `import { decode }` grew by 50 bytes gzipped.

I made strict the default because it's cheap: on 10-point lines the checks measured 0 to 4%, and nothing I could separate from the noise on longer ones. The decoder ORs every character code into one integer and checks it once at the end, and the encoder's range check also catches NaN. Most other libraries silently return a wrong last point for a truncated string; see `npm run behavior` in the benchmark repo.

#### Rounding

Encoding rounds half away from zero, as Google's algorithm description says: 0.000005 becomes 1 unit at precision 5, and -0.000005 becomes -1. That matches `@googlemaps/polyline-codec`, `@mapbox/polyline`, PostGIS and OSRM.

One difference from most JavaScript libraries: they round with `Math.floor(Math.abs(x) + 0.5)`, which turns 0.49999999999999994 (the largest double below 0.5) into 1, because the addition itself rounds up. polytini gives 0, like C's `round()` and PostGIS. It only matters for that one value at each scale.

Decoding divides by the factor instead of multiplying by its inverse, so 38.5 comes back as exactly 38.5.

### Entry points

The package picks an entry point by export condition, so you don't import these by hand:

| Condition | File | What's different |
|---|---|---|
| `workerd` | `src/deno.js` | Cloudflare Workers; the same file as deno |
| `react-native` | `src/web.js` | Metro on iOS and Android, which has no `node:buffer` |
| `bun` | `src/bun.js` | the same as node |
| `deno` | `src/deno.js` | byte buffers through TextEncoder and TextDecoder |
| `browser` | `src/browser.js` | the core, but long lines encode through TextDecoder (`dist/web.cjs` for `require` in Jest) |
| `node`, `module-sync` | `src/node.js` | Buffer-backed decode and encode |
| `default` | `src/web.js` | the portable core and nothing else |

`@duoquote/polytini/web`, `/browser` and `/node` pick one explicitly. All of them have the same API and give the same output; the test suite runs every check against each of them. `require()` gets the same files on Node 22.12 and newer and on Bun, and the CommonJS build in `dist/` elsewhere; [docs/platforms.md](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/docs/platforms.md#module-formats-and-tools) has the whole order, the fields for tools that ignore `exports`, and the CDN and `<script>` URLs.

### Streaming

`@duoquote/polytini/stream` decodes a polyline that arrives in chunks and encodes points as they come, with the same results and errors as `decode` and `encode` on the whole input, and reads one polyline per line (NDJSON included). It has TransformStreams, a `PolylineDecoder` and `PolylineEncoder` with `write` and `end`, and async iterables: [streaming.md](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/docs/streaming.md).


### Smaller: /lite

`@duoquote/polytini/lite` is `decode` and `encode` for `[lat, lng]` tuples at precision 0 to 6, and nothing else. It's the default entry's fast loops without the exact fallback paths and the options:

```js
import { decode, encode } from '@duoquote/polytini/lite';

decode('_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC');              // [[38.5, -120.2], [40.7, -120.95]]
decode(str, 6);                             // precision 6, still [lat, lng]
encode([[38.5, -120.2], [40.7, -120.95]]);  // '_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC'
```

Which one to pick: lite is for bundle size in the browser. On a server (Node, Bun, Deno) use the main entry. It's faster on long lines there, because it has the runtime's own byte paths, and the bytes don't matter.

#### Size

Gzipped bytes, each import built the same way with esbuild, Rollup (node-resolve, commonjs, terser) and webpack 5 in production mode:

| import | /lite | default entry | @placemarkio/polyline | @googlemaps/polyline-codec | @pirxpilot/google-polyline |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `decode` | 295 / 298 / 296 | 1063 / 1021 / 1043 | 230 / 236 / 234 | 252 / 247 / 245 | 305 / 302 / 300 |
| `encode` | 349 / 352 / 349 | 1432 / 1433 / 1495 | 293 / 297 / 296 | 340 / 340 / 338 | 295 / 298 / 296 |
| both | 503 / 512 / 509 | 1895 / 1907 / 1954 | 424 / 432 / 432 | 472 / 481 / 479 | 491 / 494 / 491 |

So it's a quarter of the default entry, and within about 80 bytes of the small single-purpose libraries. Those bytes buy the checks below and the speed of the default entry's loops. I tried smaller versions, and each was slower:

- A do/while decoder that appends with `push`, like most small libraries: 32 bytes smaller, and 18 to 39% slower than the core on Bun from 100 points, 5 to 11% on Node 24.
- Encoding with a loop per character instead of a table of the 1,024 shortest values: 52 bytes smaller, and 39% slower on the real-world lines on Node 24.
- `10 ** precision` instead of a table of seven factors: 16 bytes smaller, and about 50 ns per call on Node 22, a third of decoding 10 points.

#### Speed

Paired runs with `bench/ab.js --mode same` (both modules in one process, sampled in ABBA order, 10 rounds, pinned to 4 cores) and fresh Chrome contexts for Chrome. Time per call, lite divided by the other one, so 0.90 is lite 10% faster; "same" means the 95% interval included 1.00. A against itself came out within about 1% on Node and 3% in Chrome. Every call passes the precision.

Against the portable core (`/web`), which is what the default entry uses for short lines everywhere and for decoding in browsers:

| | Node 24 | Bun 1.4.3 | Deno 2.5 | Chrome 158 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| decode, 10 points | 1.03 | 0.94 | 0.93 | same |
| decode, 100 points | 0.97 | same | 0.93 | 0.94 |
| decode, real-world lines | same | same | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| decode, 10,000 points | 0.98 | same | 0.95 | 0.96 |
| encode, 10 points | 0.90 | 0.91 | 0.85 | 0.93 |
| encode, 100 points | 0.83 | 0.87 | 0.82 | 0.83 |
| encode, real-world lines | 0.92 | 0.95 | 0.93 | 0.94 |
| encode, 10,000 points | 0.88 | 0.89 | 0.88 | 0.88 |

Against each runtime's own entry, the one the bare import picks there:

| | Node 22 | Node 24 | Node 26 | Bun 1.4.3 | Deno 2.5 | Chrome 158 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| decode, 10 points | 1.01 | same | 0.92 | 0.95 | 0.91 | same |
| decode, 100 points | 1.09 | 1.05 | 1.15 | 0.96 | 0.97 | same |
| decode, real-world lines | 1.29 | 1.29 | 1.32 | 1.11 | 1.22 | same |
| decode, 10,000 points | 1.35 | 1.29 | 1.33 | 1.08 | 1.23 | same |
| encode, 10 points | 1.34 | 1.25 | 1.31 | 1.52 | 0.85 | 0.93 |
| encode, 100 points | 1.46 | 1.38 | 1.51 | 1.82 | 1.28 | 0.84 |
| encode, real-world lines | same | 0.97 | 0.95 | 1.37 | 0.95 | 0.88 |
| encode, 10,000 points | 1.43 | 1.34 | 1.30 | 1.61 | 1.36 | 1.26 |

The Node and Bun entries decode through a `Buffer` and encode into one, and Deno's decodes long lines through `TextEncoder`, so on a server the main entry is up to 1.8 times faster. In Chrome lite is as fast as the browser entry, apart from encoding long lines, where the browser entry builds the string with `TextDecoder`.

Against the small libraries it competes with on size, from 10 rounds with all five in one process (Node, Bun, Deno) or 8 rounds of fresh contexts (Chrome). Their time per call divided by lite's, so 2.0 means lite is twice as fast:

| library | runtime | decode 10 | decode 100 | decode real-world | decode 10,000 | encode 10 | encode 100 | encode real-world | encode 10,000 |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| @placemarkio/polyline | Node 24 | 1.09 | 1.16 | 1.15 | 1.10 | 1.43 | 1.43 | 2.41 | 1.80 |
| @placemarkio/polyline | Bun 1.4.3 | 1.07 | 1.38 | 1.33 | 1.22 | 1.70 | 2.11 | 1.92 | 2.36 |
| @placemarkio/polyline | Deno 2.5 | 1.12 | 1.18 | 1.17 | 1.10 | 1.43 | 1.46 | 2.36 | 1.83 |
| @placemarkio/polyline | Chrome 158 | 1.10 | same | 1.09 | same | 1.32 | 1.44 | 2.31 | 1.80 |
| @googlemaps/polyline-codec | Node 24 | 1.34 | same | 1.06 | 0.94 | 3.28 | 3.55 | 5.29 | 6.11 |
| @googlemaps/polyline-codec | Bun 1.4.3 | 1.09 | 1.14 | 1.22 | 1.08 | 4.26 | 4.58 | 4.29 | 5.42 |
| @googlemaps/polyline-codec | Deno 2.5 | 1.30 | same | 1.05 | 0.92 | 3.40 | 3.64 | 5.23 | 6.33 |
| @googlemaps/polyline-codec | Chrome 158 | 1.29 | 0.91 | 1.04 | 0.88 | 2.02 | 2.08 | 3.16 | 2.88 |
| @pirxpilot/google-polyline | Node 24 | 1.46 | 1.50 | 1.38 | 1.38 | 1.17 | 1.30 | 2.01 | 1.52 |
| @pirxpilot/google-polyline | Bun 1.4.3 | 3.10 | 3.13 | 2.74 | 3.01 | 0.94 | 1.25 | 1.48 | 1.50 |
| @pirxpilot/google-polyline | Deno 2.5 | 1.62 | 1.72 | 1.50 | 1.55 | 1.17 | 1.29 | 1.96 | 1.66 |
| @pirxpilot/google-polyline | Chrome 158 | 1.73 | 1.61 | 1.52 | 1.56 | 1.08 | 1.30 | 1.90 | 1.42 |
| google-polyline | Node 24 | 1.05 | 1.31 | 1.27 | 1.25 | 1.12 | 1.22 | 2.11 | 1.74 |
| google-polyline | Bun 1.4.3 | 1.17 | 1.51 | 1.45 | 1.34 | same | 1.11 | 1.43 | 1.66 |
| google-polyline | Deno 2.5 | 1.07 | 1.30 | 1.29 | 1.23 | 1.13 | 1.25 | 2.06 | 1.72 |
| google-polyline | Chrome 158 | 1.17 | 1.10 | 1.19 | 1.12 | 1.04 | 1.18 | 1.98 | 1.59 |

So lite is faster than `@placemarkio/polyline`, the one library that's smaller, on every runtime and line length except two Chrome cells, where they're even: 1.07 to 1.38 times for decoding and 1.32 to 2.41 times for encoding. Against all four it decodes up to 3.1 times and encodes up to 6.3 times as fast. The exceptions: `@googlemaps/polyline-codec` decodes 10,000 points 6 to 12% faster on Node, Deno and Chrome, and 100 points 9% faster in Chrome, and `@pirxpilot/google-polyline` encodes 10 points 6% faster on Bun.

#### What it checks

For everything it accepts, lite gives exactly what the default entry gives: the same numbers, the same string, the same rounding (half away from zero, exact at 0.49999999999999994) and the same division by the factor. When it can't, it throws, so it never returns a different number. `test/lite.test.js` checks this against the default entry on the vectors, the PostGIS fixture, the real-world lines and random valid and broken input, on Node, Bun, Deno, Chrome and workerd.

What each check costs in a decode-only bundle, gzipped, from `scripts/size.js`'s esbuild build:

| check | throws | bytes |
|---|---|--:|
| none (what most small libraries do) | | 245 |
| a string cut inside a value, or a latitude without a longitude | `Error('Invalid polyline')` | +31 |
| a character outside `?` to `~` | `Error('Invalid polyline')` | +11 |
| a value of 7 or more chunks, past what 32-bit math decodes | `Error('Invalid polyline')` | +5 |
| a precision other than 0 to 6 | `Error('Invalid polyline')` | +4 |
| `null` as the precision means 5, like the default entry | | +1 |

Most of the first row is the `throw` itself. In `encode`, the check for NaN, Infinity, a missing value or a coordinate past 2^29 units is 48 bytes (301 without it, 349 with). Rejecting `null` there too would be 8 more. Rounding adds 0.49999999999999994, the largest double below 0.5, and truncates, which is exact half away from zero and 16 bytes smaller than the default entry's add-0.5-and-fix.

#### Where it differs from the default entry

- The errors are plain `Error`s with the message `'Invalid polyline'` or `'Invalid coordinate'`. There's no `PolylineError`, `code` or `index`, and `err instanceof PolylineError` is false. Use the default entry if you need to tell errors apart.
- Precision is a number from 0 to 6, or `null` and `undefined` for 5. There's no options object, so no `order`, `factor`, `dimensions` or `strict: false`, and presets don't work. `decode` throws on anything else, and `encode` throws on its first point.
- Values have to fit 32-bit math. That's every valid coordinate at precision 6 and below; a value past 2^29 units (536 degrees at precision 6) throws. The default entry switches to exact Number math there instead.
- `encode` reads `p[0]` and `p[1]` of each point, so `{ lat, lng }` objects throw. `null` multiplies to 0, so `[null, 1]` encodes as `[0, 1]`, where the default entry throws. Numeric strings and booleans convert the same way in both.
- `decode` doesn't check that it got a string: `decode(123)` returns `[]`.

Without a bundler, `dist/polytini-lite.iife.js` sets the same global `polytini`, with just `decode` and `encode`.
### Detecting the encoding

A Google-format string doesn't say which precision it was written at, which coordinate comes first or how many values a point has. `@duoquote/polytini/detect` works it out from the numbers:

```js
import { detect, decodeAuto } from '@duoquote/polytini/detect';

// OSRM's polyline6 route through Berlin, from test/fixtures/presets.
detect(geometry)[0];
// { format: 'google', precision: 6, order: 'latlng', dimensions: 2,
//   presets: ['osrm6', 'valhalla', 'stadia', 'mapbox6'], confidence: 0.54, valid: true,
//   issue: null, reasons: [], options: { precision: 6, order: 'latlng', dimensions: 2 }, ... }

const { coordinates, precision, issues } = decodeAuto(geometry); // coordinates: [[lat, lng], ...]
```

The runner-up there is the same precision read longitude first, at 0.25: swapped, Berlin is at 13.4 N, 52.5 E, a plausible place too. That one sits in the Gulf of Aden, so with the land mask below the first reading gets 0.98.

`detect(str, options?)` returns every reading it tried, best first. It tries precision 5, 6, 7, 4 and 8, latitude first and longitude first, two values per point and three (elevation in centimeters, the way GraphHopper and openrouteservice write it), and HERE's Flexible Polyline when the string starts with a valid header. That's 20 Google readings, plus Flexible. Each one has:

- `format`, `precision`, `order`, `dimensions`, and `zFactor` (100) for three values per point. For Flexible they come from the header, with `thirdDim` and `thirdDimPrecision`.
- `confidence`: the reading's probability among all of them, from 0 to 1. They add up to 1.
- `valid` and `issue`: whether strict mode decodes the string this way, and if not, the `PolylineError` it throws. The issue's index is how far strict decoding got.
- `reasons`: what counted against it, like `'100% of points out of range'` or `'cut off with 3 values per point'`.
- `presets`: the presets with that precision and number of values, like `['osrm6', 'valhalla', 'stadia', 'mapbox6']`. A preset's `order` is about the tuples it gives back, not the string, so it says nothing about `order` here.
- `options`: pass them to `decode` or `decodeFlat` to get `[lat, lng]` points for this reading, whichever order the string has.

`decodeAuto(str, options?)` runs `detect`, decodes the string leniently with the best reading, and returns that reading with `coordinates`, the `issues` that `onIssue` reported (empty for a valid string) and all the `candidates`.

Options, all optional: `precisions`, `orders` and `dimensions` (arrays of what to try), `flexible: false` to skip Flexible, `isLand` (below) and `sample`.

#### How it scores

Each reading gets a score for how much its points look like real geometry, and the scores become probabilities with a softmax:

- Every point in range. A precision 6 string read at 5 gives latitudes ten times too big, usually past 90, and so does a longitude read as a latitude.
- The typical distance between points: tens to hundreds of meters scores best. It's broad on purpose, because 1 Hz walking tracks (about 1 m) and simplified overview lines (Mapbox's test response has 3.5 km steps, Google's example 250 km) are both real. A line with only a few steps counts for less here.
- No jumps 10,000 times longer than the typical step.
- Each step going on roughly in the direction of the last one. On the 1000 real-world lines the average cosine of the turns was 0.85, and under 0.54 for 1 in 100. A wrong number of values per point mixes latitude, longitude and elevation deltas, and the directions come out random: about 0.
- Elevation between -500 and 9000 m, for three values per point.
- Valid in strict mode: a reading the string is cut off under, while another isn't, loses points. Characters outside the format count against every Google reading, and digits or `-` count for Flexible.
- A prior: precision 5 is the most common, then 6, then 7, and latitude first is the format's own order.
- With `isLand`, points at sea.

The string is decoded once, with the core's `decodeFlat` at factor 1. That gives the integers every Google reading shares: a precision only divides them, an order swaps two, and three values per point regroups them. Scoring then looks at up to `sample` points (default 256) spread over the line, so a long line costs one fast decode and a fixed amount of work. On the 10,000-point benchmark track `detect` took 1.1 ms on Node 25 (where `decode` took 0.12 ms), 1.4 ms on Node 24, 0.65 ms on Bun and 1.0 ms on Deno. On the real-world lines it was about 0.3 ms per line, and at 10 points 0.02 to 0.08 ms. `decodeAuto` adds one `decode`.

#### Accuracy

`node scripts/detect-accuracy.js` (and `--land` for the mask below) prints these tables. "Right" means the best reading has the precision, order and number of values the string was written with.

| Input | Lines | Right | With `isLand` |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Real-world lines, precision 5 | 1000 | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| The same, re-encoded at precision 6 | 1000 | 99.9% | 99.9% |
| The same, re-encoded at precision 7 | 1000 | 99.9% | 99.9% |
| The same, longitude first | 1000 | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| Test vectors, decode cases with a known precision | 113 | 71.7% | 68.1% |
| PostGIS fixture: zeros, ties, bounds, one point | 116 | 44.8% | 39.7% |
| Generated tracks in 12 places, precision 5 | 600 | 100.0% | 91.7% |
| The same, precision 6 | 600 | 100.0% | 91.7% |
| The same, longitude first | 600 | 18.5% | 49.0% |
| GraphHopper's test strings with elevation | 2 | 100.0% | 100.0% |
| Generated tracks with elevation | 240 | 100.0% | 91.7% |

The real-world lines are the benchmark's 1000 routes, all in Turkey. The generated tracks are polyline-benchmark's GPS-like tracks (1 Hz, walking to highway speed, with stops), made even in meters: 50 tracks of 200 points around each place in the table below. The vectors and the PostGIS cases are edge cases by design: one or two points, zeros, the ends of the range. Many of them are the same line at more than one precision, so no reading gets all of them right.

Longitude first, per place:

| Place | Without | With `isLand` |
|---|--:|--:|
| Istanbul | 0% | 0% |
| Sao Paulo | 0% | 100% |
| Seattle | 34% | 100% |
| Sydney | 44% | 44% |
| Berlin | 0% | 100% |
| Nairobi | 0% | 100% |
| Singapore | 66% | 66% |
| Quito | 0% | 0% |
| Suva, Fiji (by the antimeridian) | 62% | 62% |
| Chukotka (by the antimeridian) | 16% | 16% |
| Svalbard (78 N) | 0% | 0% |
| McMurdo (78 S) | 0% | 0% |

#### Latitude and longitude swaps

A swapped string can only be told apart when the swapped reading is impossible or implausible, and often it's neither. When the longitude is past 90, the latitude-first reading is out of range, but the same reading at precision 6 usually isn't, and then the precision prior and the step lengths decide. That's close to a coin toss (Seattle, Sydney, Singapore). When both readings land on land, nothing in the string tells them apart: Istanbul's routes read swapped land in Saudi Arabia, which is why the real-world lines score 0% longitude first, with or without a mask. I tried right angles at turns too, which a swapped reading stretches out of shape away from the equator. It picked the right order for 75% of the real-world lines, but weighting it enough to matter cost more correct readings of normal strings than it fixed, so it's not in. If you know your data, pass `orders: ['latlng']`.

`@duoquote/polytini/detect/land` has `isLand(lat, lng)`, a 1 by 1 degree grid from Natural Earth's 1:110m land (public domain). Pass it as `detect(str, { isLand })`, or pass your own function for a finer mask. It catches swaps and precision mix-ups that land at sea: Sao Paulo, Berlin and Nairobi swapped go from 0% to 100%, Seattle from 34%. It costs too: a line the mask counts as sea loses to any reading that lands on land. That's what happens to McMurdo, on the Ross Ice Shelf, whose tracks drop to 0% at every precision, and it's the 91.7% rows. Coasts are generous (a cell counts if it has any land in it), but ice shelves and small islands missing from the 1:110m data count as sea.

So the mask isn't in `/detect` itself, and you pick it:

| Mask | Gzipped | Longitude first, generated tracks |
|---|--:|--:|
| none | 0 B | 18.5% |
| 3 degrees | 689 B | 40.7% |
| 2 degrees | 993 B | 40.7% |
| 1 degree (`/detect/land`) | 2,067 B | 49.0% |

`/detect` is 4,048 bytes gzipped: the core's decoder, `/flexible`'s decoder, the presets and the scoring. No other entry includes it. `scripts/landmask.js` builds the mask, with `--cell` for the other sizes.

#### Limits

- One polyline per call. Quotes or a trailing newline make every Google reading invalid, so trim the string first.
- A line of one or two points has little to go on beyond the range, so the prior decides most of those.
- Three values per point with an elevation that hardly changes (about 10 cm per point or less) can read as a valid two-value line with small wiggles. In the tests, with a steady climb of 10 cm per point, the two-value reading won for 1 track in 5.
- It doesn't try other `zFactor`s for the third value, `factor`s that aren't a power of ten, or more than three values per point.

## Streaming

`@duoquote/polytini/stream` encodes and decodes input that arrives in pieces:

- one long polyline in chunks, like a fetch body or a file read
- points that arrive a few at a time, encoded as they come
- many polylines, one per line, or NDJSON with a polyline field

Every class here gives exactly what `decode` and `encode` give on the whole input, wherever the chunks are cut: the same numbers, the same string, and the same `PolylineError` with the same `code`, `index` and message. It's its own entry, so the other entries didn't get bigger.

```js
import {
  PolylineDecoder, PolylineEncoder,      // write(chunk) and end(), no streams needed
  DecodeStream, EncodeStream,            // TransformStreams
  DecodeLinesStream, EncodeLinesStream,  // one polyline per line, NDJSON
  decodeIterable, encodeIterable,        // for await
  decodeLines, encodeLines,
} from '@duoquote/polytini/stream';
```

They take the same options as `decode` and `encode` (`precision`, `factor`, `order`, `strict`, `dimensions`, `zFactor`, `onIssue`, and the presets), plus `flat`.

### One long polyline in chunks

```js
const res = await fetch(url);
for await (const points of res.body.pipeThrough(new DecodeStream({ precision: 6 }))) {
  draw(points); // the points each chunk completed
}
```

`DecodeStream` takes strings or bytes and gives one array of points per chunk that completed any. Bytes are read as UTF-8, so the result is what `decode(await res.text())` would give. With `flat: true` each batch is a `Float64Array` of `[lat0, lng0, lat1, lng1, ...]`.

Without streams, `PolylineDecoder` does the same with two calls:

```js
const d = new PolylineDecoder();
d.write('_p~iF~ps|U_ul'); // [[38.5, -120.2]]
d.write('LnnqC');         // [[40.7, -120.95]]
d.end();                  // [], or throws if the input was cut off
```

A chunk can end anywhere, even inside a value. The decoder keeps only the sums so far and the value it's in the middle of.

Strict mode works the way it does in `decode`:

- An invalid character throws a `PolylineError` with code `'char'` from the `write` that reads it. The `index` is the position in the whole input, not in the chunk.
- A string that ends inside a value or a point throws `'truncated'` from `end()`, with the same index `decode` reports: the length of the input.
- A value past 2^53 throws `'overflow'`.
- Points from earlier chunks have already been returned by then. To use all of them or none, collect them and use them after `end()`.
- After an error, every call throws it again. After `end()`, the decoder starts on a new polyline.

With `strict: false` it never throws on bad data and gives what lenient `decode` gives: invalid characters are skipped and an incomplete last point is dropped. `onIssue` gets the same issues `decode` reports for the whole string, with the index in the whole input, from the `write` that reads each one (the cut-off end from `end`). See [api.md](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/docs/api.md#reporting-what-lenient-mode-skipped).

Polylines don't contain whitespace, so a file that ends with a newline fails in strict mode, like `decode` does on it. For text with one polyline per line, use `DecodeLinesStream`.

### Points to a string

```js
const e = new PolylineEncoder({ precision: 6 });
let s = e.write([38.5, -120.2]);             // one point
s += e.write([[40.7, -120.95], [43.252, -126.453]]); // or an array of them
s += e.end();
// s === encode(allPoints, 6)
```

`write` takes one point (a tuple or a `{ lat, lng }` object) or an array of points, and returns the string for them. An array whose first item isn't an object is one tuple. With `flat: true` it takes flat arrays of numbers, and a point can be split between two writes. Errors are `encode`'s, with the point's index in the whole input.

`EncodeStream` is the same as a TransformStream:

```js
points.pipeThrough(new EncodeStream()).pipeTo(writable);
```

### Many polylines, one per line

```js
const res = await fetch('/routes.ndjson');
const lines = res.body.pipeThrough(new DecodeLinesStream({ field: 'shape', precision: 6, errors: 'skip', onError: (err, line) => console.warn(line, err.message) }));
for await (const route of lines) show(route.id, route.shape);
```

`DecodeLinesStream` reads text or bytes with one polyline per line (`\n` or `\r\n`) and gives one result per line: its points, or with `field` the line's JSON object with that field decoded. Blank lines are skipped, and whitespace around a polyline is ignored. A line can be split between chunks anywhere.

A bad line errors the stream by default, with the `PolylineError` (or `SyntaxError` for bad JSON) and the 1-based line number as `err.line`; `err.index` is the position in the line. With `errors: 'skip'` the line is left out and the error goes to `onError(err, line)`. With `strict: false`, `onIssue` gets each line's issues with the index in the line and the line number as `line`.

`EncodeLinesStream` goes the other way: one array of points (or one object, with `field`) per chunk in, one line of text out, with a `\n`.

### Async iterables

For sources that aren't web streams: async generators, Node Readables, arrays.

```js
for await (const [lat, lng] of decodeIterable(fs.createReadStream('route.txt'))) { /* ... */ }
for await (const piece of encodeIterable(points)) out.write(piece);
for await (const route of decodeLines(fs.createReadStream('routes.txt'))) { /* ... */ }
```

- `decodeIterable(chunks, options)` yields one point at a time. That's convenient but costs an `await` per point; `DecodeStream` and `PolylineDecoder` give whole batches.
- `encodeIterable(points, options)` takes points or arrays of points and yields the string in pieces of about 64 KB. For a piece as soon as each point arrives, use `PolylineEncoder`.
- `decodeLines` and `encodeLines` are the line streams as async generators.

They also take a ReadableStream, and read it with a reader where `for await` on streams isn't supported (older Safari versions). The `for await` loops over `pipeThrough` in this page need that support; `decodeIterable(res.body)` doesn't.

### Node streams

Node 18 and up have the web streams as globals, so the classes work as they are. To connect them to Node streams:

```js
import { Readable, Duplex } from 'node:stream';
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises';

// A Node Readable into a web stream
Readable.toWeb(fs.createReadStream('routes.txt')).pipeThrough(new DecodeLinesStream());

// A web TransformStream as a Node Duplex, in a pipeline
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream('route.txt'), Duplex.fromWeb(new DecodeStream(), { objectMode: true }), sink);

// Or an async generator, which pipeline takes as a step
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream('route.txt'), (src) => decodeIterable(src), sink);
```

All three work on Node 22 to 26 and Bun 1.4. In Deno, use its web streams directly: its `Duplex.fromWeb` threw an internal error after a failed pipeline when I tried it. This entry doesn't import `node:stream`, so browser bundles stay clean.

React Native has no TransformStream. There `PolylineDecoder`, `PolylineEncoder` and the iterables work, and constructing a `DecodeStream` throws a TypeError that says so.

### Speed

The decoder uses the same 2D loop as `decode` for whole points and falls back to the exact per-character code only for a point split between chunks, other dimensions and bad input. The tuple loop stops 12 characters before the end of each chunk, since a point it reads is at most 12 characters long, so it never reads past the chunk and needs no count. The flat one counts the points first, like `decodeFlat`, to size its array.

Measured with `bench/ab.js` (paired, separate processes, 8 rounds, high priority on 4 pinned cores) on 1,000,000 points cut into 64 KB chunks, against one call on the whole input. B/A below 1 means streaming was faster. A against itself gave 0.97 (0.93 to 1.02) and 0.96 (0.93 to 0.99) on Node 25, so differences of a few percent are noise.

String chunks against `decode` (or `encode`) on the whole string. Encoding writes 4,096 points at a time:

| Runtime | decode | decodeFlat | encode | encodeFlat |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Node 22.9 | 1.066 (1.019 to 1.116) | 1.125 (0.992 to 1.276) | 0.355 (0.331 to 0.381) | 0.351 (0.334 to 0.369) |
| Node 24.10 | 1.009 (0.961 to 1.061) | 0.953 (0.901 to 1.008) | 1.117 (1.106 to 1.129) | 1.020 (0.989 to 1.052) |
| Node 25.2 | 1.034 (1.011 to 1.057) | 1.041 (1.026 to 1.056) | 1.089 (1.062 to 1.117) | 1.031 (1.016 to 1.046) |
| Bun 1.4.3 | 0.914 (0.891 to 0.938) | 0.803 (0.788 to 0.818) | 1.146 (1.098 to 1.196) | 1.152 (1.091 to 1.217) |
| Deno 2.5.4 | 1.072 (1.052 to 1.092) | 0.997 (0.941 to 1.056) | 1.061 (1.039 to 1.084) | 1.015 (0.992 to 1.039) |

Byte chunks, the way a fetch body or a file read comes, against `decode(await res.text())`, which turns all the bytes into one string first:

| Runtime | decode | decodeFlat |
|---|--:|--:|
| Node 22.9 | 1.083 (1.048 to 1.119) | 1.187 (1.159 to 1.217) |
| Node 24.10 | 1.000 (0.928 to 1.078) | 0.987 (0.917 to 1.062) |
| Node 25.2 | 1.042 (1.029 to 1.055) | 1.034 (0.999 to 1.071) |
| Bun 1.4.3 | 0.933 (0.916 to 0.950) | 0.868 (0.835 to 0.901) |
| Deno 2.5.4 | 1.040 (1.018 to 1.063) | 1.010 (0.973 to 1.049) |

In headless Chrome 157, timed in the page (10 rounds, A and B alternating first, the fastest of 15 calls each): 0.943 (0.894 to 0.995) for `decode`, 1.116 (1.098 to 1.133) for `decodeFlat`, and 0.727 (0.549 to 0.963) for byte chunks against `res.text()`.

So decoding through the stream costs 0 to 8% on V8 and is faster on Bun; flat output costs up to 19% on Node 22. Encoding on Node 22 is almost three times as fast in pieces, because one 1,000,000-point string built with `+=` is slow to flatten there. The numbers include reading each output piece once (`--consume full`) and, for decoding, not copying the batches into one array, since a consumer uses them as they come. The commands:

```sh
node bench/ab.js --a src/web.js --b bench/stream.js --cases decode:1000000,decodeFlat:1000000,encode:1000000,encodeFlat:1000000 --rounds 8 --samples 20 --warm 500 --consume full --prio high --affinity 0xF000
STREAM_CHUNKS=bytes node bench/ab.js --a bench/stream-text.js --b bench/stream.js --cases decode:1000000,decodeFlat:1000000 --rounds 8 --samples 20 --warm 500 --consume full --prio high --affinity 0xF000
```

with `--exe` for the other runtimes. On the 1000 real-world lines, one `PolylineDecoder` per line (write, then end) took 2.93 ms against 2.73 ms for `decode`, the fastest of 40 interleaved runs in one Node 25 process: about 7% more, most of it the decoder's setup.

### Size

Gzipped with `node scripts/size.js`: 3,721 bytes for the whole entry, 1,782 for `PolylineDecoder` alone. The CLI, which uses it, is 6,987.

### How it's tested

`test/stream.test.js` checks the property above directly. For random valid polylines (any precision, order, 1 to 3 dimensions, strict and lenient), broken ones (cut, a bad character, a value past 2^53, characters outside ASCII), random strings, the 183 decode vectors, the 380 PostGIS decode cases in both coordinate orders and the 1,000 real-world lines, it cuts the input at every position, as a string and as UTF-8 bytes, and at random chunk sizes, and compares the points and the error with `decode` and `decodeFlat` on every entry. Encoding is checked the same way with the points split into every two batches, random batches, one point per write and flat values cut anywhere. It runs on Node 22 to 26, Bun, Deno, headless Chrome and workerd.

## Integrations

Each one is its own subpath, so none of them add bytes to the main entry. None of them import their map library either: you pass it in (`install(L)`, `createPolylineFormat({ Polyline, LineString })`), or they only return data the library takes. Their type files import the library's types, which TypeScript finds in your own install.

### Presets for routing engines

```js
import { decode, toGeoJSON } from '@duoquote/polytini';
import { osrm6, valhalla, graphhopper3d } from '@duoquote/polytini/presets';

decode(route.geometry, osrm6);          // [[lng, lat], ...], same as geometries=geojson
decode(leg.shape, valhalla);            // Valhalla and Stadia shapes, precision 6
toGeoJSON(path.points, graphhopper3d);  // GraphHopper elevation=true: [lng, lat, ele]
decode(path.points, { ...graphhopper3d, factor: path.points_encoded_multiplier });
```

`google`, `osrm`, `osrm6`, `valhalla`, `stadia`, `graphhopper`, `graphhopper3d`, `openrouteservice`, `openrouteservice3d`, `mapbox`, `mapbox6`, `strava` and `otp`. Each one is a plain options object with the precision, the order the engine uses for its own coordinates, and the elevation factor where there is one. The sources are cited in `src/presets.js`. Decoding matches every engine exactly. Encoding can differ by one unit from GraphHopper and openrouteservice on negative exact halves, and from OpenTripPlanner, which floors.

### Leaflet

A real plugin for Leaflet 1.9 and the Leaflet 2 betas, and a superset of the old `Polyline.encoded.js` plugin:

```js
import L from 'leaflet';
import { install } from '@duoquote/polytini/leaflet';
install(L); // or: import '@duoquote/polytini/leaflet/auto' when Leaflet is the global L

const line = L.Polyline.fromEncoded(str, { color: 'red', precision: 6 }).addTo(map);
line.toEncoded();                                  // '...'
L.Polygon.fromEncoded([outer, hole]).toEncoded();  // ['...', '...']
L.polylineEncoded(str).addTo(map);                 // factories, Leaflet 1.9 only
```

Multi-polylines and polygons with holes are arrays of strings. Leaflet 2 exports a frozen module namespace, so there `install` adds the static and prototype methods but skips the lower-case factories.

On a page without a bundler, Leaflet is often a `<script>` tag. polytini's IIFE (`dist/polytini.iife.js`, see [CDNs](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/docs/platforms.md#cdns)) has the main API as the global `polytini`, not the plugin, so there `L.polyline(polytini.decode(str))` draws the line.

### Turf

```js
import { toFeature, toFeatureCollection, fromGeoJSON } from '@duoquote/polytini/turf';

turf.length(toFeature(str, { precision: 6, properties: { id: 1 }, bbox: true }));
fromGeoJSON(turf.simplify(toFeature(str), { tolerance: 0.001 })); // ['...']
```

`fromGeoJSON` takes any GeoJSON and returns one string per line: LineStrings, MultiLineString parts and polygon rings. There's also `toPolygonFeature(rings)` for Google-style encoded polygons.

### Google Maps

A drop-in for `google.maps.geometry.encoding.decodePath` and `encodePath`:

```js
import { decodePath, encodePath } from '@duoquote/polytini/google';

const path = decodePath(route.polyline.encodedPolyline); // LatLng[] once Maps has loaded
new google.maps.Polyline({ path, map });
encodePath(polyline.getPath());                           // MVCArray<LatLng> to string
decodePath(str, { LatLng: false });                       // {lat, lng} literals, in Node too
```

It's strict by default too. Google's documentation doesn't say what `decodePath` does with bad input.

### OpenLayers

A subclass of `ol/format/Polyline`, with the same options and output. You pass in ol's classes, so polytini doesn't import ol:

```js
import Polyline from 'ol/format/Polyline.js';
import LineString from 'ol/geom/LineString.js';
import { createPolylineFormat } from '@duoquote/polytini/openlayers';

const FastPolyline = createPolylineFormat({ Polyline, LineString }); // or createPolylineFormat(ol) with the full build
const format = new FastPolyline({ factor: 1e6 });
const feature = format.readFeature(route.geometry, { featureProjection: 'EPSG:3857' });
```

On Node 25 it read 1.1 to 1.8 times and wrote 1.2 to 1.9 times as fast as ol's own format, depending on line length (`node --expose-gc bench/openlayers.js`). One thing it fixes: ol's own `writeGeometry` overwrites the geometry's coordinates with the deltas when no projection change is involved, so writing the same geometry twice gives garbage. This one leaves the geometry alone. Unusual input (bad strings, huge values, tile-pixel projections) goes to ol's own methods on a copy, so the output stays identical to ol's.

### MapLibre GL and Mapbox GL

```js
import { addPolylineLayer, setPolylineData } from '@duoquote/polytini/maplibre'; // or /mapbox
import { osrm6 } from '@duoquote/polytini/presets';

map.on('load', () => addPolylineLayer(map, 'route', route.geometry, { ...osrm6, layer: { paint: { 'line-width': 4 } } }));
setPolylineData(map, 'route', [a.geometry, b.geometry], { ...osrm6, properties: [{ name: 'a' }, { name: 'b' }] });
```

`polylineSource()` and `polylineData()` build the GeoJSON source and FeatureCollection without touching a map. Both map libraries take the same calls, so `/mapbox` re-exports `/maplibre` with Mapbox's types. On JSR, where the types can't import maplibre-gl or mapbox-gl, the map parameter is a structural `MapLike` that any real `Map` fits; before 0.1.5 it rejected them. `test/fixtures/jsr` checks every JSR type file against the real libraries' objects.

### deck.gl

Decodes straight into deck.gl's binary attribute format, with one buffer for all lines and no array per point:

```js
import { PathLayer } from '@deck.gl/layers';
import { binaryPaths } from '@duoquote/polytini/deckgl';

const data = binaryPaths(routes.map((r) => r.geometry), { precision: 6, float32: true });
new PathLayer({ id: 'routes', data, _pathType: 'open', getWidth: 3, widthUnits: 'pixels' });
```

`binaryPolygons()` does the same for polygon fills. In deck.gl 9.4 the composite `PolygonLayer` doesn't take binary data, so use `SolidPolygonLayer`, plus a `PathLayer` over the same buffer for outlines. TripsLayer timestamps come out as a Float32Array, because a Float64Array drew nothing.

### HERE Flexible Polyline

A different format, with a header and an optional third dimension, fully separate from the Google-format code:

```js
import { encode, decode, ELEVATION } from '@duoquote/polytini/flexible';

const str = encode({ polyline: [[50.10228, 8.69821, 112.5], [50.10201, 8.69567, 113.1]], precision: 5, thirdDim: ELEVATION, thirdDimPrecision: 1 });
const { precision, thirdDim, polyline } = decode(str);
```

The same arguments and results as `@here/flexpolyline`, so it's a drop-in. Unlike it, `decode` also takes `{ strict: false, onIssue }`: it then skips invalid characters and drops a cut-off last point, like the Google-format decoders, and tells `onIssue` about each. A bad header always throws. It matches every line of HERE's official test data, including precision 11 and up, where `@here/flexpolyline` itself doesn't.

## CLI

```sh
pnpm dlx @duoquote/polytini decode "kviyHviWkCbkBsg@guA"
```

```sh
bunx @duoquote/polytini encode 51.5007,-0.1246 51.5014,-0.1419 51.5079,-0.1281
```

```sh
deno run -R jsr:@duoquote/polytini/cli decode -p 6 -f geojson --file route.txt
```

```sh
yarn dlx @duoquote/polytini decode "kviyHviWkCbkBsg@guA"
```

```sh
npx @duoquote/polytini decode --lines --file routes.txt
```

The first two use the same three points in London, Westminster, Buckingham Palace and Trafalgar Square, one in each direction: `decode` prints `[[51.5007,-0.1246],[51.5014,-0.1419],[51.5079,-0.1281]]` and `encode` prints `kviyHviWkCbkBsg@guA`. Deno needs `-R` (`--allow-read`) only for `--file`.

`yarn dlx` needs Yarn 2 or newer; on Yarn 1, use `npx`. It prints Yarn's install log to stdout before the output, so add `-q` when you pipe it: `yarn dlx -q @duoquote/polytini decode ...`.

Yarn 4.19 and newer won't install a package version that's less than a day old (the `npmMinimalAgeGate` setting, 1440 minutes by default). So for a day after each release, `yarn dlx @duoquote/polytini` fails with `YN0016: The version for tag "latest" is quarantined`. Use `npx` or another launcher until then, or pin a version that's at least a day old: `yarn dlx @duoquote/polytini@<version> ...`. If you'd rather take the new release right away, `YARN_NPM_MINIMAL_AGE_GATE=0` turns the check off for that command.

I ran every command on this page in cmd, PowerShell 5.1 and Git Bash, with each of the five launchers (Yarn 4.19 for `yarn dlx`).

### Quoting

The examples work as written in every shell. Your own polylines can contain `` ` ``, `\`, `|` and `^`, which shells treat specially, so quote them:

- bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell: single quotes, `` '_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@' ``
- cmd: double quotes, `` "_p~iF~ps|U_ulLnnqC_mqNvxq`@" ``

A polyline never contains `'`, `"`, `$`, `%` or `!`, so these quotes always work, with one exception: in cmd, a polyline that ends in `\` needs that last backslash doubled, `"...fw\\"`, because Windows programs read `\"` as a quote character. polytini says so when it sees one. Double quotes in bash, zsh and PowerShell only work for polylines without `` ` `` and `\`. To skip quoting altogether, put the polyline in a file and use `--file`.

Coordinates for `encode` need no quotes: `51.5007,-0.1246` passes through every shell as it is. In PowerShell an unquoted pair reaches the command as `51.5007 -0.1246`, which polytini reads the same way.

### Input

`encode` takes `lat,lng` pairs as arguments (`lng,lat` with `--lnglat`). Otherwise both commands read `--file <path>` or stdin, and `-` or `--file -` also mean stdin:

- `decode` reads one polyline per line. Blank lines and whitespace around a polyline are ignored.
- `encode` reads JSON (`[[lat, lng], ...]`, several lines of points, or GeoJSON), CSV with a `lat` and a `lng` (or `lon`, `longitude`) column, or `lat,lng` lines without a header. GeoJSON is always `[lng, lat]`.

Input is read in chunks and output written as it's ready, so a polyline of a million points needs about as much memory as a small one. Two exceptions: JSON input to `encode` is read whole, since it's one value, and when `decode` reads more than one line from stdin without `--lines`, it keeps the first line's text until it sees a second one, because the output for one polyline and for several looks different. With `--file` it reads the file twice instead.

Output for a small input is written all at once at the end, so a command that fails prints nothing but the error. Past 1 MB of output, or with `--lines`, it's written as it goes, and an error stops it with what came before already printed.

### One per line

`--lines` reads one input per line and writes one output per line, so a file of any number of lines goes through with constant memory:

```sh
npx @duoquote/polytini decode --lines --file routes.txt
```

```sh
npx @duoquote/polytini encode --lines --file points.ndjson
```

- `decode --lines` prints each line's points as JSON (`-f json`), a GeoJSON LineString (`-f geojson`), CSV rows with the line's index (`-f csv`), or `lat,lng` pairs separated by spaces (`-f lines`), the same format `encode` takes as arguments.
- `encode --lines` reads a JSON array of points, a GeoJSON LineString or Feature, or `lat,lng` pairs separated by spaces, per line.
- `--field <name>` reads each line as a JSON object (NDJSON) and decodes or encodes only that field, leaving the rest of the object as it is. It implies `--lines`.

```sh
npx @duoquote/polytini decode --field shape -p 6 --file trips.ndjson
```

A bad line stops the command with exit code 1 and says which line it was: `polytini: line 3: Invalid character at 0`. With `--skip-errors` it reports the line and goes on.

Instead of `--file`, stdin works too: `< routes.txt` or `cat routes.txt |` in bash, `< routes.txt` or `type routes.txt |` in cmd, and `Get-Content routes.txt |` in PowerShell, which has no `<`.

### Options

Installed in a project, the command is `polytini`:

```
polytini 0.1.9: encode and decode Google encoded polylines

Usage:
  polytini encode [lat,lng ...] [options]
  polytini decode [polyline ...] [options]

Input is the arguments, --file <path>, or stdin (also - or --file -).

  encode takes lat,lng pairs as arguments, or reads JSON ([[lat, lng], ...],
         or GeoJSON), CSV with a header, or "lat,lng" lines, and prints one
         polyline per line.
  decode reads one polyline per line and prints coordinates.

Options:
  -p, --precision <n>  decimal places, 0 to 15 (default 5; OSRM polyline6
                       and Valhalla use 6)
      --lnglat         coordinates are [lng, lat], like GeoJSON (GeoJSON
                       input is always read that way)
      --no-strict      accept malformed input instead of failing
  -f, --format <fmt>   decode output: json (default), geojson, csv or lines
      --file <path>    read input from a file
      --lines          one input per line, one output per line (NDJSON)
      --field <name>   with --lines: each line is a JSON object and this
                       field holds the polyline or the coordinates
      --skip-errors    with --lines: report a bad line and go on
  -h, --help           show this help
  -v, --version        show the version

Examples:
  polytini decode "kviyHviWkCbkBsg@guA"
  polytini encode 51.5007,-0.1246 51.5014,-0.1419 51.5079,-0.1281
  polytini decode -p 6 -f geojson --file route.txt
  polytini decode --lines --file routes.txt
  polytini encode --file points.csv

Polylines can contain \ ` | and ^, which shells treat specially. Quote
them: single quotes in bash, zsh, fish and PowerShell, double quotes in cmd.
```

It has no dependencies and isn't part of the library entry points, so it adds nothing to them. It decodes and encodes with the same code as [`@duoquote/polytini/stream`](https://github.com/Duoquote/polytini/blob/main/docs/streaming.md).
